Minimal mass blow up solutions for a double power nonlinear Schrödinger equation

Stefan Le Coz Address: Institut de Mathématiques de Toulouse,

Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We consider a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with double power nonlinearity

i​∂tu+Δ​u+|u|4d​u+ϵ​|u|p−1​u=0,ϵ∈{−1,0,1}, 1<p<4di\partial_{t}u+\Delta u+|u|^{\frac{4}{d}}u+\epsilon|u|^{p-1}u=0,\ \ \epsilon\in\{-1,0,1\},\ \ 1<p<\frac{4}{d}

in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (d=1,2,3d=1,2,3). Classical variational arguments ensure that H1​(ℝd)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) data with ‖u0‖2<‖Q‖2\|u_{0}\|_{2}<\|Q\|_{2} lead to global in time solutions, where QQ is the ground state of the mass critical problem (ϵ=0\epsilon=0). We are interested by the threshold dynamic ‖u0‖2=‖Q‖2\|u_{0}\|_{2}=\|Q\|_{2} and in particular by the existence of finite time blow up minimal solutions. For ϵ=0\epsilon=0, such an object exists thanks to the explicit conformal symmetry, and is in fact unique from the seminal work [22]. For ϵ=−1\epsilon=-1, simple variational arguments ensure that minimal mass data lead to global in time solutions. We investigate in this paper the case ϵ=1\epsilon=1, exhibiting a new class of minimal blow up solutions with blow up rates deeply affected by the double power nonlinearity. The analysis adapts the recent approach [31] for the construction of minimal blow up elements.

Key words and phrases: 
blow-up, nonlinear Schrödinger equation, double power nonlinearity, minimal mass, critical exponent

1. Introduction

We consider the following double power nonlinear Schrödinger equation in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}

(NLS){i​∂tu+Δ​u+|u|4d​u+ϵ​|u|p−1​u=0,u|t=0=u0,​ 1<p<1+4d,ϵ∈{−1,0,1}.{\rm(NLS)}\ \ \left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}i\partial_{t}u+\Delta u+|u|^{\frac{4}{d}}u+\epsilon|u|^{p-1}u=0,\\ u_{|t=0}=u_{0},\end{array}\right.\ \ 1<p<1+\frac{4}{d},\ \ \epsilon\in\{-1,0,1\}. (1)

This model corresponds to a subcritical perturbation of the classical mass critical problem ϵ=0\epsilon=0 which rules out the scaling symmetry of the problem. It is well-known (see e.g [6] and the references therein) that for any u0∈H1​(ℝd)u_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), there exists a unique maximal solution u∈𝒞⁡((−T⋆,T⋆),H1​(ℝd))u\in\mathcal{C}((-T_{\star},T^{\star}),H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})) ∩\cap 𝒞1​((−T⋆,T⋆),H−1​(ℝd))\mathcal{C}^{1}((-T_{\star},T^{\star}),H^{-1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})) of (1). Moreover, the mass (i.e. L2L^{2} norm) and energy EE of the solution are conserved by the flow where:

E⁡(u)=12​∥∇u∥22−12+4d​∥u∥2+4d2+4d−ϵ​1p+1​∥u∥p+1p+1.E(u)=\frac{1}{2}\lVert\nabla u\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{1}{2+\frac{4}{d}}\lVert u\rVert_{2+\frac{4}{d}}^{2+\frac{4}{d}}-\epsilon\frac{1}{p+1}\lVert u\rVert_{p+1}^{p+1}.

Moreover, there holds the blow up criterion:

T⋆<+∞implieslimt↑T⋆∥∇u​(t)∥2=+∞.T^{\star}<+\infty\ \ \mbox{implies}\ \ \lim_{t\uparrow T^{\star}}\lVert\nabla u(t)\rVert_{2}=+\infty. (2)

In this paper, we are interested in the derivation of a sharp global existence criterion for (1) in connection with the existence of minimal mass blow up solutions of (1).

1.1. The mass critical problem

Let us briefly recall the structure of the mass critical problem ϵ=0\epsilon=0. In this case, the scaling symmetry

uλ​(t,x)=λd2​u​(λ2​t,λ​x)u_{\lambda}(t,x)=\lambda^{\frac{d}{2}}u(\lambda^{2}t,\lambda x)

acts on the set of solutions and leaves the mass invariant

‖uλ​(t,⋅)‖2=‖u⁡(λ2​t,⋅)‖2.\|u_{\lambda}(t,\cdot)\|_{2}=\|u(\lambda^{2}t,\cdot)\|_{2}.

From variational argument [32], the unique ([3, 14]) up to symmetry ground state solution to

−ΔQ+Q−|Q|4dQ=0,Q∈H1(ℝd),Q>0,Q radial-\Delta Q+Q-|Q|^{\frac{4}{d}}Q=0,\ \ Q\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\ \ Q>0,\ \ \mbox{$Q$ radial}

attains the best constant in the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality

‖u‖2+4d2+4d≤C​‖u‖24d​‖∇u‖22,\|u\|^{2+\frac{4}{d}}_{{2+\frac{4}{d}}}\leq C\|u\|_{2}^{\frac{4}{d}}\|\nabla u\|_{2}^{2},

so that

∀u∈H1​(ℝd),Ecrit=12​∥∇u∥22−12+4d​∥u∥2+4d2+4d≥12​‖∇u‖22​[1−(‖u‖2‖Q‖2)4d].\forall u\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\ \ E_{\rm crit}=\frac{1}{2}\lVert\nabla u\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{1}{2+\frac{4}{d}}\lVert u\rVert_{2+\frac{4}{d}}^{2+\frac{4}{d}}\geq\frac{1}{2}\|\nabla u\|_{2}^{2}\left[1-\left(\frac{\|u\|_{2}}{\|Q\|_{2}}\right)^{\frac{4}{d}}\right]. (3)

Together with the conservation of mass and energy and the blow up criterion (2), this implies the global existence of all solutions with data ‖u0‖2<‖Q‖2\|u_{0}\|_{2}<\|Q\|_{2}. In fact, there holds scattering, see [10] and references therein.
At the threshold ‖u0‖2=‖Q‖2\|u_{0}\|_{2}=\|Q\|_{2}, the pseudo-conformal symmetry

1|t|d2​u​(1t,xt)​ei​|x|24​t\frac{1}{|t|^{\frac{d}{2}}}u\left(\frac{1}{t},\frac{x}{t}\right)e^{i\frac{|x|^{2}}{4t}} (4)

applied to the solitary wave solution u⁡(t,x)=Q⁡(x)​ei​tu(t,x)=Q(x)e^{it} yields the existence of the following explicit minimal blow up solution

S(t,x)=1|t|d2Q(x|t|)e−i​|x|24​|t|ei|t|,∥S(t)∥2=∥Q∥2,∥∇S(t)∥2∼t∼0−1|t|.S(t,x)=\frac{1}{|t|^{\frac{d}{2}}}Q\left(\frac{x}{|t|}\right)e^{-i\frac{|x|^{2}}{4|t|}}e^{\frac{i}{|t|}},\quad\|S(t)\|_{2}=\|Q\|_{2},\quad\|\nabla S(t)\|_{2}\mathop{\sim}_{t\sim 0^{-}}\frac{1}{|t|}. (5)

From [22], minimal blow up elements are classified in H1​(ℝd)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) in the following sense

‖u⁡(t)‖2=‖Q‖2andT∗<+∞implyu≡S\|u(t)\|_{2}=\|Q\|_{2}\ \ \mbox{and}\ \ T^{*}<+\infty\ \ \mbox{imply}\ \ u\equiv S

up to the symmetries of the flow. Note that the minimal blow up dynamic (5) can be extended to the super critical mass case ‖u0‖2>‖Q‖2\|u_{0}\|_{2}>\|Q\|_{2} (see [5]) and that it corresponds to an unstable threshold dynamics between global in time scattering solutions and finite time blow up solutions in the stable blow up regime

‖∇u​(t)‖2​∼t∼T∗log⁡|log⁡|T∗−t||T∗−t.\|\nabla u(t)\|_{2}\mathop{\sim}_{t\sim T^{*}}\sqrt{\frac{\log|\log|T^{*}-t||}{T^{*}-t}}. (6)

We refer to [26] and references therein for an overview of the existing literature for the L2L^{2} critical blow up problem.

1.2. The case ϵ=−1\epsilon=-1

Let us now consider the case of a defocusing perturbation. First, there are no solitary waves with subcritical mass ‖u0‖2<‖Q‖2\|u_{0}\|_{2}<\|Q\|_{2} from a standard Pohozaev integration by parts argument. At the threshold, we claim:

Lemma 1 (Global existence at threshold for ϵ=−1\epsilon=-1).

Let ϵ=−1\epsilon=-1. Let u0∈H1​(ℝd)u_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) with ‖u0‖2=‖Q‖2\|u_{0}\|_{2}=\|Q\|_{2}, then the solution of (1) is global and bounded in H1​(ℝd)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

The proof follows from standard concentration compactness argument, see Appendix A. The global existence criterion of Lemma 1 is sharp in the sense that for all α∗>0\alpha^{*}>0, we can build an H1​(ℝd)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) finite time blow up solution to (7) with ‖u0‖2=‖Q‖2+α∗\|u_{0}\|_{2}=\|Q\|_{2}+\alpha^{*} and blow up speed given by the log-log law (6). This is a consequence of the strong structural stability of the log log regime and the proof would follow the lines of [28, 29, 30].

1.3. The case ϵ=1\epsilon=1

We now turn to the case ϵ=1\epsilon=1 for the rest of the paper, i.e. we consider the model

i​∂tu+Δ​u+|u|4d​u+|u|p−1​u=0where1<p<1+4d.i\partial_{t}u+\Delta u+|u|^{\frac{4}{d}}u+|u|^{p-1}u=0\quad\hbox{where}\quad 1<p<1+\frac{4}{d}. (7)

First, from mass and energy conservation, using (3) and (72), H1​(ℝd)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) solutions with ‖u0‖2<‖Q‖2\|u_{0}\|_{2}<\|Q\|_{2} are global and bounded in H1​(ℝd)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). However, large time scattering is not true in general, even for small L2L^{2} solutions, since there exist arbitrarily small solitary waves.

Lemma 2 (Small solitary waves).

For all M∈(0,‖Q‖2)M\in(0,\|Q\|_{2}), there exists ω⁡(M)>0\omega(M)>0 and a Schwartz radially symmetric solution of

Δ​QM−ω⁡(M)​QM+QM1+4d+QMp=0,‖QM‖2=M.\Delta Q_{M}-\omega(M)Q_{M}+Q_{M}^{1+\frac{4}{d}}+Q_{M}^{p}=0,\ \ \|Q_{M}\|_{2}=M.

The proof follows from classical variational methods, see Appendix B.

The main result of this paper is the existence of a minimal mass blow up solution for (7), in contrast with the defocusing case ϵ=−1\epsilon=-1.

Theorem 1 (Existence of a minimal blow up element).

Let d=1,2,3d=1,2,3 and 1<p<1+4d1<p<1+\frac{4}{d}. Then for all energy level E0∈ℝE_{0}\in\mathbb{R}, there exist t0<0t_{0}<0 and a radially symmetric Cauchy data u⁡(t0)∈H1​(ℝd)u(t_{0})\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) with

‖u⁡(t0)‖2=‖Q‖2,E⁡(u⁡(t0))=E0,\|u(t_{0})\|_{2}=\|Q\|_{2},\ \ E(u(t_{0}))=E_{0},

such that the corresponding solution u⁡(t)u(t) of (7) blows up at time T∗=0T^{*}=0 with speed:

‖∇u​(t)‖2=C​(p)+ot↑0​(1)|t|σ\|\nabla u(t)\|_{2}=\frac{C(p)+o_{t\uparrow 0}(1)}{|t|^{\sigma}} (8)

for some universal constants

σ=44+d⁡(p−1)∈(12,1),C⁡(p)>0.\quad\sigma=\frac{4}{4+d(p-1)}\in\left(\tfrac{1}{2},1\right),\ \ C(p)>0.

Comments on the result.

1. On the existence of minimal elements. Since the pioneering work [22], it has long been believed that the existence of a minimal blow up bubble was related to the exceptional pseudo conformal symmetry (4), or at least to the existence of a sufficiently sharp approximation of it, see [2, 16]. However, a new methodology to construct minimal mass elements for a inhomogeneous (NLS) problem, non perturbative of critical (NLS), was developed in [31], and later successfully applied to problems without any sort of pseudo conformal symmetry, [4, 12, 19]. More generally, the heart of the matter is to be able to compute the trajectory of the solution on the soliton manifold, see [13, 18] for related problems for two solitary waves motion. The present paper adapts this approach which relies on the direct computation of the blow up speed and the control of non dispersive bubbles as in [15].

Observe that the blow up speed (8) is quite surprising since it approaches the self simiar blow up speed |t|−12{|t|^{-\frac{1}{2}}} as p→(1+4d)−p\to\left(1+\frac{4}{d}\right)^{-}.

2. Uniqueness. A delicate question investigated in [4, 19, 31] is the uniqueness of the minimal blow up element. Such a uniqueness statement should involve Galilean drifts since the Galilean symmetry applied to (7) is an L2L^{2} isometry and automatically induces minimal elements with non trivial momentum. Uniqueness issues lie within the general question of classifying the compact elements of the flow in the Kenig-Merle road map [11]. A more limited question is to determine the global behavior of the minimal element for negative time, which is poorly understood in general. Here, at least in the case E0≥0E_{0}\geq 0, one can see from Virial type estimates that the solution is global in negative time.

3. Detailed structure of the singular bubble. The analysis provides the following detailed structure of the blow up bubble

u⁡(t,x)=1λd2​(t)​Q​(xλ⁡(t))​e−i​σ​|x|24​t​ei​γ​(t)+v⁡(t,x)u(t,x)=\frac{1}{\lambda^{\frac{d}{2}}(t)}Q\left(\frac{x}{\lambda(t)}\right)e^{-i\sigma\frac{|x|^{2}}{4t}}e^{i\gamma(t)}+v\left(t,{x}\right) (9)

where QQ is the mass critical ground state, and

limt→0∥v(t)∥2=0,λ(t)∼Cp|t|σas t→0−,\lim_{t\rightarrow 0}\lVert v(t)\rVert_{2}=0,\quad\lambda(t)\sim C_{p}{|t|^{\sigma}}\quad\hbox{as $t\to 0^{-}$},

for some constant Cp>0C_{p}>0. Note also that the dimension restriction d∈{1,2,3}d\in\{1,2,3\} is for the sake of simplicity but not essential.

The construction of the minimal blow up element for (1) can be viewed as part of a larger program of understanding what kind of blow up speeds are possible for (NLS) type models. Let us repeat that log-log type solutions with super critical mass can be constructed for (1), but then the question becomes: do these examples illustrate all possible blow up types, at least near the ground state profile? The recent series of works [19, 20, 21] for the mass critical gKdV equation indicate that this is a delicate problem, and that the role played by the topology used to measure the perturbation is essential. More generally, symmetry breaking perturbations are very common in nonlinear analysis, and while they are expected to be lower order for generic stable blow up dynamics, our analysis shows that they can dramatically influence the structure of unstable threshold dynamics such as in our case minimal blow up bubbles.

1.4. Notation

Let us collect the main notation used throughout the paper. For the sake of simplicity, we work in the radial setting only. The L2L^{2} scalar product and LqL^{q} norm (q≥1q\geq 1) are denoted by

(u,v)2=Re⁡(∫ℝdu⁡(x)​v¯​(x)​𝑑x),‖u‖q=(∫ℝd|u|q)1q.\left(u,v\right)_{2}=\mathrm{Re}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}u(x)\bar{v}(x)dx\right),\quad\|u\|_{q}=\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|u|^{q}\right)^{\frac{1}{q}}.

We fix the notation:

f⁡(z)=|z|4d​z;g⁡(z)=|z|p−1​z;F⁡(z)=14d+2​|z|4d+2;G⁡(z)=1p+1​|z|p+1.f(z)=|z|^{\frac{4}{d}}z;\quad g(z)=|z|^{p-1}z;\quad F(z)=\frac{1}{\frac{4}{d}+2}|z|^{\frac{4}{d}+2};\quad G(z)=\frac{1}{p+1}|z|^{p+1}.

Identifying ℂ\mathbb{C} with ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, we denote the differential of these functions by d​fdf, d​gdg, d​FdF and d​GdG. Let Λ\Lambda be the generator of L2L^{2}-scaling i.e.

Λ=d2+y⋅∇.\Lambda=\frac{d}{2}+y\cdot\nabla.

The linearized operator close to QQ comes as a matrix

L+:=−Δ+1−(1+4d)​Q4d,L−:=−Δ+1−Q4d.L_{+}:=-\Delta+1-\left(1+\frac{4}{d}\right)Q^{\frac{4}{d}},\qquad L_{-}:=-\Delta+1-Q^{\frac{4}{d}}.

and the generalized kernel of

(0L−−L+0)\begin{pmatrix}0&L_{-}\\ -L_{+}&0\end{pmatrix}

is non-degenerate and spanned by the symmetries of the problem (see [14, 33] for the original results and [8] for a short proof). It is completely described in Hrad1​(ℝd)H^{1}_{\rm rad}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) by the relations (we define ρ\rho as the unique radial solution to L+​ρ=|y|2​QL_{+}\rho=|y|^{2}Q)

L−​Q=0,L+​Λ​Q=−2​Q,L−​|y|2​Q=−4​Λ​Q,L+​ρ=|y|2​Q.L_{-}Q=0,\quad L_{+}\Lambda Q=-2Q,\quad L_{-}|y|^{2}Q=-4\Lambda Q,\quad L_{+}\rho=|y|^{2}Q. (10)

Denote by 𝒴\mathcal{Y} the set of radially symmetric functions f∈𝒞∞​(ℝd)f\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that

∀α∈ℕd,∃Cα,κα>0,∀x∈ℝd,|∂αf⁡(x)|≤Cα​(1+|x|)κα​Q​(x).\forall\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{d},\quad\exists C_{\alpha},\ \kappa_{\alpha}>0,\ \forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\quad|\partial^{\alpha}f(x)|\leq C_{\alpha}(1+|x|)^{\kappa_{\alpha}}Q(x).

It follows from the kernel properties of L+L_{+} and L−L_{-}, and from well-known properties of the Helmholtz kernel (see [1] for the properties of Helmholtz kernel (i.e. Bessel and Hankel functions) and [9, Appendix A] or proof of Lemma 3.2 in [27] for related arguments) that

∀g∈𝒴,∃f+∈𝒴,L+​f+=g,\displaystyle\forall g\in\mathcal{Y},\ \exists f_{+}\in\mathcal{Y},\ L_{+}f_{+}=g, (11)
∀g∈𝒴,(g,Q)2=0,∃f−∈𝒴,L−​f−=g.\displaystyle\forall g\in\mathcal{Y},\ \left(g,Q\right)_{2}=0,\ \exists f_{-}\in\mathcal{Y},\ L_{-}f_{-}=g. (12)

Throughout the paper, CC denotes various positive constants whose exact values may vary from line to line but are of no importance in the analysis. When an inequality is true up to such a constant, we also use the notation ≲\lesssim, ≳\gtrsim or ≈\approx.

2. Construction of the blow-up profile

In this section, we define the blow-up profile which is relevant to construct the minimal mass solution – see Proposition 3 below.

2.1. Blow up profile

Let us start with some heuristic arguments justifying the construction. As usual in blow up contexts, we look for a solution of the following form, with rescaled variables (s,y)(s,y):

u⁡(t,x)=1λd2​(s)​w​(s,y)​ei​γ​(s)−i​b⁡(s)​|y|24,d​sd​t=1λ2,y=xλ⁡(s),u(t,x)=\frac{1}{\lambda^{\frac{d}{2}}(s)}w(s,y)e^{i\gamma(s)-i\frac{b(s)|y|^{2}}{4}},\qquad\frac{ds}{dt}=\frac{1}{\lambda^{2}},\qquad y=\frac{x}{\lambda(s)},

where the function ww, and the time dependent parameters λ>0\lambda>0, bb and γ\gamma are to be determined satisfying the following equation

i​ws+Δ​w−w+f⁡(w)+λα​g​(w)−i⁡(b+λsλ)​Λ​w+(1−γs)​w+(bs+b2)​|y|24​w−b⁡(b+λsλ)​|y|22​w=0,iw_{s}+\Delta w-w+f(w)+\lambda^{\alpha}g(w)\\ -i\left(b+\frac{\lambda_{s}}{\lambda}\right)\Lambda w+(1-\gamma_{s})w+(b_{s}+b^{2})\frac{|y|^{2}}{4}w-b\left(b+\frac{\lambda_{s}}{\lambda}\right)\frac{|y|^{2}}{2}w=0, (14)

where

α=2−d⁡(p−1)2∈(0,2).\alpha=2-\frac{d(p-1)}{2}\in(0,2).

Since we look for blow up solutions, the parameter λ⁡(s)\lambda(s) should converge to zero as s→∞s\to\infty. Therefore,

w⁡(s,y)=Q⁡(y),b+λsλ=bs+b2=1−γs=0w(s,y)=Q(y),\qquad b+\frac{\lambda_{s}}{\lambda}=b_{s}+b^{2}=1-\gamma_{s}=0 (15)

is a solution of (14) at the first order, i.e. when neglecting λα​|w|p−1​w\lambda^{\alpha}|w|^{p-1}w. However, the first order error term λα​Qp\lambda^{\alpha}Q^{p} cannot be neglected in the minimal mass blow up analysis (while it could be neglected easily in the log-log regime where λ∼e−ecb\lambda\sim e^{-e^{\frac{c}{b}}}). Therefore, starting from QQ, we need to look for a refined blow up ansatz. Actually, to close the analysis for any α∈(0,2)\alpha\in(0,2), we need to remove error terms at any order of λα\lambda^{\alpha} and bb in the equation of ww. It is important to note that in the process of constructing the approximate solution, we cannot exactly solve (14) since we need to introduce new terms in the equation (due to degrees of freedom necessary to construct the ansatz) that will modify the modulation equations in (15). These terms (gathered in the time dependent function θ⁡(s)\theta(s) below) are responsible for the specific blow up law obtained in Theorem 1.

Fix K∈ℕK\in\mathbb{N}, K≫1K\gg 1 (K>20/αK>20/\alpha is sufficient in the proof of Theorem 1), and

ΣK={(j,k)∈ℕ2|j+k≤K}.\Sigma_{K}=\{(j,k)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\ |\ j+k\leq K\}.
Proposition 3.

Let λ⁡(s)>0\lambda(s)>0 and b⁡(s)∈ℝb(s)\in\mathbb{R} be 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} functions of ss such that λ⁡(s)+|b⁡(s)|≪1\lambda(s)+|b(s)|\ll 1.
(i) Existence of a blow up profile. For any (j,k)∈ΣK(j,k)\in\Sigma_{K}, there exist real-valued functions Pj,k+∈𝒴P_{j,k}^{+}\in\mathcal{Y}, Pj,k−∈𝒴P_{j,k}^{-}\in\mathcal{Y} and βj,k∈ℝ\beta_{j,k}\in\mathbb{R} such that P⁡(s,y)=P~K​(y,b⁡(s),λ⁡(s))P(s,y)=\tilde{P}_{K}(y;b(s),\lambda(s)), where P~K\tilde{P}_{K} is defined by

3. Existence proof assuming uniform estimates

This section is devoted to the proof of Theorem 1 by a compactness argument, assuming uniform estimates on specific solutions of (7). These estimates are given in Proposition 7.

3.1. Uniform estimates in rescaled time variable

5. The mixed energy Morawetz monotonicity formula

In this section, following [31], we introduce a mixed Energy/Morawetz functional to control the remaining part of the solution in H1​(ℝd)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). First, define the energy of ε\varepsilon

H⁡(s,ε):=12​∥∇ε∥22+12​∥ε∥22−∫ℝd(F⁡(Pb+ε)−F⁡(Pb)−d​F​(Pb)​ε)​𝑑y−λα∫ℝd(G(Pb+ε)−G(Pb)−dG(Pb)ε)dy.H(s,\varepsilon):=\frac{1}{2}\lVert\nabla\varepsilon\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\lVert\varepsilon\rVert_{2}^{2}-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(F(P_{b}+\varepsilon)-F(P_{b})-dF(P_{b})\varepsilon)dy\\ -\lambda^{\alpha}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(G(P_{b}+\varepsilon)-G(P_{b})-dG(P_{b})\varepsilon)dy.

Note that as in [31], the time derivative of the linearized energy HH for ε\varepsilon cannot be controlled alone, and one has to add a virial type functional such as b2Im∫ℝd∇(|y|22)∇εε¯dy.\frac{b}{2}\mathrm{Im}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\nabla\left(\frac{|y|^{2}}{2}\right)\nabla\varepsilon\bar{\varepsilon}dy. In practice, due to the lack of control on ∥y​ε∥2\lVert y\varepsilon\rVert_{2}, we replace 12​|y|2\frac{1}{2}|y|^{2} by a function whose gradient is bounded, which we introduce now.
Let ϕ:ℝ→ℝ\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be a smooth even and convex function, nondecreasing on ℝ+\mathbb{R}^{+}, such that

ϕ(r)={12​r2 for r<1,3​r+e−r for r>2,\phi(r)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{1}{2}r^{2}&\text{ for }&r<1,\\ &3r+e^{-r}&\text{ for }&r>2,\end{aligned}\right.

and set ϕ⁡(x)=ϕ⁡(|x|)\phi(x)=\phi(|x|). Let A≫1A\gg 1 to be fixed. Define ϕA\phi_{A} by ϕA​(y)=A2​ϕ​(yA)\phi_{A}(y)=A^{2}\phi\left(\frac{y}{A}\right) and

J(ε)=12Im∫ℝd∇ϕA⋅∇εε¯dy.J(\varepsilon)=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Im}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\nabla\phi_{A}\cdot\nabla\varepsilon\bar{\varepsilon}dy.

Finally, set

S⁡(s,ε)=1λ4​(s)​(H⁡(s,ε)+b⁡(s)​J​(ε⁡(s))).S(s,\varepsilon)=\frac{1}{\lambda^{4}(s)}(H(s,\varepsilon)+b(s)J(\varepsilon(s))).

The relevance of the functional SS lies on the following two properties.

Proposition 10 (Coercivity of SS).

Proposition 11.

dd​s​[S⁡(s,ε⁡(s))]≳bλ4​(s)​(∥ε⁡(s)∥H12+O⁡(s−2​(K+1))CLOSE.\frac{d}{ds}\left[S(s,\varepsilon(s))\right]\gtrsim\frac{b}{\lambda^{4}(s)}\left(\lVert\varepsilon(s)\rVert_{H^{1}}^{2}+O(s^{-2(K+1)}\right).

The rest of this section is organized as follows. We first prove Proposition 10 in §5.1. In §5.2 we compute the time derivative of HH and in §5.3, the time derivative of JJ. We finish the proof of Proposition 11 in §5.4.
